stages.name: External shocks and policy
stages.title: External shocks and policy
stages.sub: You can explain why external shocks are hard for policymakers to control and evaluate the response.

steps.q: A war in another country suddenly doubles the world price of oil. Did anything the UK government or Bank of England did cause this?
steps.right: No, it came from outside the economy
steps.wrong: Yes, it followed from a domestic policy decision
steps.hint: Think about where the war and the oil price rise actually happened.
steps.pre: An unexpected event starting outside the domestic economy that hits it anyway is an

steps.q: A pandemic shuts down world trade and a sudden global recession hits import demand. Are both of these the same kind of event as the oil price war?
steps.right: Yes, both start outside the domestic economy
steps.wrong: No, only one of them counts as external
steps.hint: Ask where each event originates, not what it affects.
steps.pre: Pandemics, wars, global recessions and commodity price swings are all examples of

steps.q: Oil prices have doubled, pushing up costs and prices across the economy. Government spending and tax changes, interest rate changes, and letting the currency move are all available. Does only one of these tools exist for tackling this?
steps.right: No, several different tools could be used
steps.wrong: Yes, there is really only one option
steps.hint: Fiscal, monetary and exchange rate policy are all separate tools sitting there unused.

steps.q: The Bank of England raises interest rates to bring inflation from the oil shock back down. What is this an example of?
steps.right: Using a macro policy tool to react to the shock
steps.wrong: A tool that removes the shock from happening again
steps.hint: Does raising rates stop the war, or does it deal with the effects of the war on the economy?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: The Bank of England raises interest rates today. Does the fall in inflation happen today, or only after many months?
steps.hint: Interest rate changes take time to affect spending, and spending takes time to affect prices.

steps.q: Using the AD/AS model, a sudden rise in import costs shifts aggregate supply left, raising prices and lowering output. If the interest rate rise arrives many months later, could it undo both problems well, given raising rates also reduces demand and output further?
steps.right: No, it may fix inflation but worsen the fall in output
steps.wrong: Yes, it fixes both problems equally well
steps.hint: Higher rates cut demand. Does cutting demand help an economy where output has already fallen?

steps.q: After all this, could the government have used any policy to stop the war or the pandemic from happening in the first place?
steps.right: No, those events were outside its control
steps.wrong: Yes, with the right policy mix it could have prevented them
steps.hint: Policy can react to the shock's effects, but can it reach the actual cause abroad?
